concept.body: In every parallelogram the diagonals bisect EACH OTHER: their crossing point O is the midpoint of both, so AO = OC and BO = OD. That's the only universal diagonal property — equal diagonals (rectangle), perpendicular diagonals (rhombus), and angle-bisecting diagonals (rhombus) are upgrades that general parallelograms don't carry.

explanationVariants: O is the midpoint of BD: OD = BO = 11, and BD = 22.
The halves of one diagonal match: OD = 11.

widget.prompt: Diagonals meet at O; BO = 11. Find OD.

commonErrors.feedback: 22 is the FULL diagonal BD. OD is the other half, equal to BO: 11.
5.5 halves the half — BO is already a half. Its partner OD matches it: 11.

steps.body: Draw BOTH diagonals and mark their crossing point O. Alternate interior angles plus the opposite sides we've already proved congruent make the small triangles across O congruent (ASA) — and CPCTC lands the third jewel: **the diagonals bisect each other.** Each diagonal cuts the other exactly in half at O.

widget.prompt: Turn on 'Inspect midpoints' and watch the two diagonal midpoints. Move D until ABCD is a parallelogram, and see what the two dots do when it becomes one.
widget.successFeedback: The two dots have landed on each other at (5, 3). That single point is what 'the diagonals bisect each other' buys you: the midpoint of AC and the midpoint of BD are not merely close, they are the same point, so each diagonal cuts the other into two equal halves.
widget.positionFeedback: D is not at (3, 5) yet, and the two midpoint dots are still apart. Two separate dots means each diagonal is cutting the other somewhere off-centre — which is exactly what bisection rules out.
widget.evidenceFeedback: Turn on 'Inspect midpoints' and move D a few times before checking. One position is not evidence: the claim is that the dots merge for a parallelogram and separate for everything else, and you have to see both halves of that.

predict.prompt: In a parallelogram, the midpoint of diagonal AC and the midpoint of diagonal BD are…

options.label: Close together, but generally different points
At opposite ends of the shape

predict.reveal: The same point. That is what makes 'bisect each other' a single fact rather than two: one crossing point that is simultaneously the middle of both diagonals, giving AO = OC and BO = OD in one stroke.

explanationVariants: The other diagonal halves AC at O: 9.

widget.prompt: Diagonal AC of a parallelogram measures 18, meeting BD at O. Find AO.

commonErrors.feedback: 18 is the WHOLE diagonal — O sits at its midpoint, so AO is half: 9.
36 doubles it — backwards. From whole to half: 18/2 = 9.

explanationVariants: O is BD's midpoint too: BD = 2 × BO = 14.
The halves match (BO = OD = 7), so the whole is 14.

widget.prompt: In the same parallelogram, BO = 7. Find the full diagonal BD.

commonErrors.feedback: 7 is only the HALF from B to O — the diagonal continues equally beyond: BD = 14.
28 doubles the whole — BO is a half, so one doubling suffices: 2 × 7 = 14.

steps.body: Keep the guarantees straight, because the specials will blur them: a general parallelogram's diagonals **need not be equal** (that's the rectangle's badge), **need not be perpendicular**, and **need not bisect the corner angles** (both are the rhombus's badges). The one universal diagonal fact is the mutual halving.

explanationVariants: Only the mutual bisection is universal; equal length and perpendicularity are special-parallelogram upgrades.
Every parallelogram halves its diagonals at the crossing; rectangles and rhombi add extra perks.

widget.prompt: Which diagonal property holds in EVERY parallelogram?

options.label: They bisect each other
options.feedback: The four-small-triangles ASA argument works in every parallelogram — mutual halving is universal.

options.label: They are equal in length
options.feedback: Equal diagonals is the RECTANGLE's signature — skew a rectangle and one diagonal stretches while the other shrinks.

options.label: They are perpendicular
options.feedback: Perpendicular diagonals mark the RHOMBUS. A long, low parallelogram crosses its diagonals at a shallow angle.

options.label: They bisect the corner angles
options.feedback: Angle-bisecting diagonals also belong to the RHOMBUS. The universal fact is that each diagonal halves the other.

widget.prompt: AO = 2x + 3 and OC = x + 8 on diagonal AC of a parallelogram. Which equation finds x?

options.label: 2x + 3 = x + 8
options.feedback: O is the midpoint of AC, so its two halves are EQUAL — set them equal and solve.

options.label: (2x + 3) + (x + 8) = 180
options.feedback: 180 is for supplementary ANGLES — these are lengths. Midpoint means the halves match: 2x + 3 = x + 8.

options.label: 2x + 3 = 2(x + 8)
options.feedback: Neither half doubles the other — they're the SAME size. Plain equality: 2x + 3 = x + 8.

options.label: (2x + 3)(x + 8) = AC
options.feedback: Halves ADD to the whole; they never multiply. And for x, just equate them: 2x + 3 = x + 8.

hints: The whole diagonal is TWICE the half.
explanationVariants: x = 5 makes AO = OC = 13, so AC = 26.
Solve (x = 5), evaluate a half (13), double for the whole: 26.

widget.prompt: With AO = 2x + 3 and OC = x + 8, find the FULL diagonal AC.

commonErrors.feedback: 5 is x — the question asks the diagonal's LENGTH. Each half is 13, so AC = 26.
13 is one HALF (AO). The diagonal spans both halves: 2 × 13 = 26.

takeaways: Parallelogram diagonals bisect each other: AO = OC and BO = OD.
They need NOT be equal, perpendicular, or angle-bisecting — those are rectangle/rhombus upgrades.
Midpoint equalities turn diagonal expressions into equations; remember to answer for the length asked.
